SEC16A-01.explanation: In an "either ... or" subject, the verb agrees with the member closer to it. Here that member is "several of her nestmates," which is plural, so the verb must be plural even though the first member, "a lone scout," is singular and "either" can feel singular. The sentence also opens with "Ever since the first cards were placed," which describes an action continuing from a past starting point up to the present, so the present perfect is required: "have hauled." "has hauled" has the right aspect but is singular, agreeing with "a lone scout" rather than with the nearer member. "had hauled" is a past perfect, which needs a later past moment to look back from; here the span runs up to the present ("is eaten," "is discarded"). "were hauling" is plural but past progressive, which describes an action in progress at some past moment and does not fit the span from a starting point up to now set up by "Ever since."

SEC16A-02.explanation: Because the sentence begins with the limiting phrase "Only in the decades since ...," the auxiliary comes before the subject. That subject is "the long-standing and once nearly universal textbook assumption," whose head noun, "assumption," is singular; the plural "vents" just before the blank belongs to the fronted phrase and is not the subject. The period "in the decades since" runs up to the present, which the present-tense "are fueled" confirms, so the present perfect is needed: "has ... begun." "have" is plural, agreeing with "vents" or "submersibles" rather than with "assumption." "had" forms the past perfect, which needs a later past moment to look back from; the passage gives none, since the period extends to now. "did" cannot combine with the participle "begun."

SEC16A-03.explanation: The relative pronoun "that" refers to "shoots": it is the shoots, not their "revival," that have sat in sealed envelopes since the collection was assembled (a revival happens only when the shoots are rewetted). Because "shoots" is plural, the verb in the relative clause must be plural. The shoots are also acted upon (someone preserved them), and no object follows the verb, so the passive voice is needed: "have been preserved." "has been preserved" is passive but singular, agreeing with the distant "revival" (or with "collection"). "have preserved" is plural but active, which would require an object stating what the shoots preserved. "has preserved" is both singular and active.

SEC16A-04.explanation: In a sentence beginning with "there," the verb agrees with the subject that follows it. Here the subject comes only after the intervening phrase "under a layer of brittle glue applied by some thrifty binder": it is "both a strip ... and a fragment ...," a compound subject, so the verb must be plural. The passage narrates a past discovery ("lifted," "expected," "was still legible"), so the verb must be past tense: "were still concealed." "was still concealed" is past but singular, as if "binder," "glue," or the first item "a strip" alone were the subject. "have long been concealed" is plural but present perfect, which describes a state continuing up to now; the passage narrates a finished past discovery, after which the fragments were no longer concealed. "has long been concealed" is singular and present perfect.

SEC16A-05.explanation: The sentence opens with "Had one researcher not taken the unusual step ...," an inverted form of "If one researcher had not taken ...." This describes a condition contrary to what happened in the past, so the main clause must state an unreal past result with "would have" plus a past participle: "would have been dismissed." "would be dismissed" expresses an unreal present or general result, not the past outcome the passage describes ("could then be seen"). "will have been dismissed" is a future perfect, which states a real future outcome and cannot complete a contrary-to-fact past condition. "had been dismissed" is past perfect indicative, which presents the dismissal as something that actually happened and leaves the "Had ..." clause without a conditional result.

SEC16A-06.explanation: The subject "Most tagged fish" has three verbs joined in a series: "drifted downstream ...," "lingered for days ...," and the verb in the blank. Items in such a series must be parallel, and the first two are simple past, so the third must be too: "headed out to sea." "heading out to sea" is a participle; joined by "and" to two finite verbs it leaves the series unbalanced and cannot serve as the fish's third action. "had headed out to sea" is past perfect, which breaks the parallel series and wrongly places the departure before the earlier steps, although the passage says it came last, "only after" the gills changed. "head out to sea" is the base (present) form, which conflicts with the past-tense verbs in the series.

SEC16A-07.explanation: The colon after "three sources" introduces a series of three items, and each item contains its own comma: "rye sourdough starters, some of them maintained ...," "kefir grains, a dairy culture from the Caucasus," and "rice wine cakes, which are dried ...." When series items contain internal commas, semicolons must separate the items so that the reader can tell where each one ends: "generations; kefir grains, a dairy culture from the Caucasus; and." "generations, kefir grains, a dairy culture from the Caucasus, and" uses commas as separators, so the separators cannot be told apart from the commas inside the items, and "a dairy culture from the Caucasus" reads as a fourth source. "generations: kefir grains, a dairy culture from the Caucasus: and" adds colons inside a series that the earlier colon has already introduced; a colon cannot separate list items. "generations kefir grains, a dairy culture from the Caucasus and" leaves no separator at all, running the first item into the second and the second into the third.

SEC16A-08.explanation: The first sentence says the engraver made "more than a dozen plates" of the cactus, so "the engraver's plate" alone does not identify which plate botanists rely on; the title "Midnight Bloom" is needed to pick it out. A title that identifies one of several is restrictive and takes no punctuation before it: "plate "Midnight Bloom,"" (the comma after the title simply precedes the "because" clause). "plate, "Midnight Bloom,"" sets the title off with commas, treating it as extra information about the engraver's only plate, which contradicts the first sentence. "plate—"Midnight Bloom,"" opens a dash interruption mid-sentence that is never closed with a second dash, and it too treats the title as nonessential. "plate; "Midnight Bloom,"" uses a semicolon, which must join independent clauses, but the words that follow it (a title and a "because" clause) cannot stand as a sentence.

SEC16B-01.explanation: The subject of the verb is the singular noun "The mortar"; the phrase "including its white lumps of lime and its glassy volcanic fragments" is set off by commas and does not change the subject's number, so the verb must be singular. The verb must also be active, because the mortar does something to an object: after the parenthetical "a team of materials scientists has argued," the clause continues with "the hairline cracks that seawater opens," which is the direct object. "repeatedly seals" is singular and active, so it is correct. "repeatedly seal" is active but plural; it agrees with "fragments" rather than with "The mortar." "is repeatedly sealed" is singular but passive, which leaves "the hairline cracks" with no grammatical role in the clause. "are repeatedly sealed" is both plural and passive.

SEC16B-02.explanation: With a fraction such as "two-thirds of," the verb agrees with the noun after "of." Here that noun is "carbon," a singular mass noun, so the verb must be singular even though "two-thirds" sounds plural and the sentence is crowded with plural nouns ("cores," "marshes," "signatures"). The verb must also be passive: the carbon does not bring anything; it was carried into the marsh by the tides, and nothing in the rest of the clause ("into the marsh from elsewhere, carried in on the tides...") can serve as an object for an active "bring." "was actually brought" is singular and passive, so it is correct. "were actually brought" is passive but plural, agreeing with "two-thirds" or "cores" instead of "carbon." "had actually brought" is active, so it would make the carbon the bringer of something, and the clause supplies no object. "actually brought" can only be read as active past (again with no object) or as a participle modifying "carbon," which would leave the clause after "found that" with no main verb at all.

SEC16B-03.explanation: The subject is "The two notebooks," which is plural. When "each" follows a plural subject rather than serving as the subject itself, it does not make the verb singular: "The two notebooks ... each are," not "each is." The verb must also be passive. The notebooks are not doing the digitizing; the passage names who is ("volunteers photograph a few pages every week"), and nothing in the clause after the blank ("at a separate library, one near the valley and one in a distant capital") can serve as the object an active "digitizing" requires. "are now being digitized" is plural and passive, so it is correct. "is now being digitized" is passive but singular, treating "each" as the subject. "are now digitizing" is plural but active, making the notebooks the ones digitizing something with no object. "is now digitizing" is both singular and active.

SEC16B-04.explanation: The clause "the water breaks through a bank and carves a new route to the sea" is already complete, and only a comma follows it, so the blank must begin a modifying phrase rather than a new verb of the same subject. A present participle phrase does this and expresses the result of the flood: "leaving riverside towns along the abandoned channel without the waterway." "left riverside towns" and "had left riverside towns" are finite verbs; each would add a third predicate to "breaks ... and carves" with only a comma and no conjunction, and their past tenses also clash with the present tense "breaks" and "carves." "having left riverside towns" is nonfinite, but the perfect participle places the leaving before the main action, which is illogical: the towns are stranded as a result of the new route, not before it.

SEC16B-05.explanation: The engineer's assurance is reported with a past-tense verb, "assured," and it concerned something that, from the time of the assurance, still lay ahead: the wall had not yet been built ("hired ... to design"). A future seen from a past point is expressed with "would" plus the base verb. The later sentences confirm that the whole episode is in the past and that the prediction has already been tested and failed ("The opposite occurred," "the town was paying dredging crews"), so "would keep out" is correct. "will keep out" speaks from the present about a still-open future, which contradicts the narrative showing the outcome is already known. "keeps out" uses the present tense for an event that, at the time of the assurance, had not happened. "had kept out" places the keeping out before the assurance, when the wall did not yet exist.

SEC16B-06.explanation: The subject, "the age of even one seed," is the thing that is measured, not the thing doing the measuring, and the rest of the clause ("with remarkable precision from a fragment smaller than a speck of dust") contains no object for an active verb. The verb must therefore be passive. The passage describes what is generally true now ("are among," "turns," "survives"), so a present modal fits: "can be determined." "can determine" is active, making the age the one that determines something and leaving the verb without an object. "has determined" is likewise active and objectless. "had been determined" is passive but past perfect, which requires an earlier past reference point; the passage is set in the general present, so it does not fit.

SEC16B-07.explanation: The words before the blank form a complete independent clause that announces something ("One designer countered the problem with a feature that is invisible at normal reading distance yet obvious under magnification"), and the words after it identify that feature: "deep notches at each such junction that give the excess ink room to spread." A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation, so "magnification: deep" is correct. "magnification; deep" is wrong because a semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "deep notches at each such junction ..." has no main verb ("give" belongs to the relative clause "that give"). "magnification, deep" makes the noun phrase an appositive renaming "magnification," which is illogical: the notches are the feature, not the magnification. "magnification deep" runs the two noun phrases together with no punctuation, producing an ungrammatical string.

SEC16B-08.explanation: The sentence opens with a list of three noun phrases ("Cold water, acid released by the moss, and an almost complete absence of oxygen") that has no verb of its own; the main clause is "any one of these conditions would slow the bacteria," whose subject sums up the list. A dash is the mark that sets a fronted list off from a clause that resumes it, so "oxygen—any" is correct. "oxygen. Any" is wrong because the period would end a sentence consisting only of the list, which has no verb and is therefore a fragment. "oxygen, any" leaves the list dangling, attached to the clause by a comma with no grammatical role, since the clause already has its own subject ("any one of these conditions"). "oxygen any" runs the list straight into the clause with no punctuation, which is ungrammatical.
